question.prompt: The numbers \(\log(a^3 b^7),\) \(\log(a^5 b^{12}),\) and \(\log(a^8 b^{15})\) are the first three terms of an arithmetic sequence, and the \(12\)th term of the sequence is \(\log(b^n).\) What is \(n?\)

solutions.explanation:
Logarithm rules turn the products and powers into linear expressions. The positive logarithm arguments force \(a>0\), from \(a^5b^{12}>0\), and then \(b>0\), from \(a^3b^7>0\). Set
\[
u=\log a,\qquad v=\log b.
\]
The first three terms are \(3u+7v\), \(5u+12v\), and \(8u+15v\). In an arithmetic sequence, twice the middle term equals the sum of its neighbors, so
\[
2(5u+12v)=(3u+7v)+(8u+15v).
\]
Simplifying gives \(u=2v\). The first term is therefore \(13v\), and the common difference is
\[
(5u+12v)-(3u+7v)=2u+5v=9v.
\]
The twelfth term lies eleven common differences after the first, so it is
\[
13v+11(9v)=112v.
\]
Because \(\log(b^n)=nv\), the stated equality requires
\[
(n-112)v=0.
\]
If \(b\ne1\), then \(v\ne0\), and division by \(v\) gives \(\boxed{n=112}\), choice D.

If \(b=1\), however, then \(v=0\) and \(u=2v=0\), so \(a=1\). Every term of the sequence is then zero, and \(\log(1^n)=0\) for every listed value of \(n\). Thus the displayed statement does not determine a unique answer; choice D is the unique answer only with the additional condition \(b\ne1\).
solutions.title: Work with the logarithms of the variables
